name: Adam
title: The first human and the ancestor of humanity
summary: As the first human, Adam occupies a unique place in the biblical narrative. Formed from the dust of the earth and given the breath of life directly by God (Gen 2:7), he was placed to care for Eden's garden, name the animals, and live in close fellowship with his Creator. When he and Eve broke God's command by eating from the tree of knowledge, they were driven out of the garden—an event that initiated the reign of sin and death over humanity (Gen 3). Adam's role extends far beyond Genesis: as the ancestor of all mankind and the one who brought sin into the world, he stands in New Testament theology as the great counterpart to Jesus Christ. Where the first Adam brought fall and death, the last Adam—Christ—brought righteousness, reconciliation, and eternal life (Rom 5:12–21; 1 Cor 15:22,45).
roles: steward of the Garden of Eden

keyEvents.title: The Creation of Adam
keyEvents.description: God formed Adam from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, so that he became a living soul—the first human, created in God's image.

keyEvents.title: The Mission in the Garden of Eden
keyEvents.description: God placed Adam in the Garden of Eden to work it and take care of it. He was free to eat from any tree, but was warned not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil—on that day he would die.

keyEvents.title: Naming the Animals
keyEvents.description: God brought all the beasts of the field and the birds of the sky to Adam so that he might name them. In this process it became clear that none of the creatures was a suitable helper for him.

keyEvents.title: Eva is Created
keyEvents.description: God caused Adam to fall into a deep sleep, took one of his ribs, and formed the woman. When Adam saw her, he exclaimed: 'This is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.'

keyEvents.title: The Fall
keyEvents.description: The serpent tempted Eve to eat from the forbidden fruit, and she also gave some to Adam, who ate. Their eyes were opened, they realized their nakedness, and God confronted them with the consequences: pain, toil, and ultimately death. They were driven out of the Garden of Eden.

keyEvents.title: Adam's Descendants and Death
keyEvents.description: Adam had sons and daughters, including Cain, Abel, and Seth. He lived 930 years and died—a confirmation of God's word that disobedience leads to death.

versions.summary: Adam was the first human, created by God from the dust of the ground and given the breath of life. He was placed to work and care for the Garden of Eden and to name all the animals. Together with Eve he fell into sin by eating from the tree of knowledge, which brought death and corruption into the world.

versions.summary: Adam was the first human, created by God from the dust of the earth and given breath of life (Gen 2:7). He was placed to cultivate and keep the garden of Eden, to name all the animals, and to steward creation. Together with Eve he fell into sin by eating from the tree of knowledge, which brought sin, death, and corruption into the world. Adam holds a central place in salvation history as the ancestor of all humanity and as a typological counterpart to Christ: through the first Adam came death, but through the last Adam – Jesus Christ – came resurrection and life (Rom 5:12–21; 1 Cor 15:22,45).

footnotes.text: The name 'Adam' (Hebrew: אָדָם, 'adam') is closely related to the word 'adamah' (אֲדָמָה), which means 'ground' or 'earth.' This wordplay highlights humanity's origin from the earth and its close connection to creation (Gen 2:7). Some scholars also point to a possible connection with the Hebrew word 'adom' (אָדוֹם), meaning 'red,' possibly referring to the color of the soil from which humans were formed.

In Jewish tradition (Talmud, Sanhedrin 38b), Adam's creation is described as a twelve-hour process on the sixth day: in the first hour dust was gathered, then he was shaped, given life, and finally named. This detailed account reflects the rabbinic interest in expanding upon biblical narratives.

Paul uses Adam as a typological counterpart to Christ in Rom 5:12–21. Just as sin and death entered the world through the first Adam, righteousness and life came through the last Adam, Jesus Christ (cf. 1 Cor 15:22,45). This Adam-Christ typology is a central theme in Pauline theology and has been foundational for Christian doctrines of original sin and atonement.
According to Gen 5:4, Adam had sons and daughters beyond the three named sons Cain, Abel, and Seth. Rabbinic tradition speculates on the number of children, with some sources mentioning up to 70.

In Mesopotamian creation literature, such as the Atrahasis epic and Enuma Elish, there are parallels to the story of humanity's creation from dust or clay. These texts provide an important cultural and literary context for the biblical creation account, even though the theological framework is fundamentally different—the Bible presents humans as created in God's image with unique dignity.

The Hebrew verb 'yatsar' (יָצַר), used to describe God forming Adam in Gen 2:7, is the same word used for a potter shaping clay. This imagery highlights the personal and craftsmanship nature of God's creation of humanity, in contrast to the more impersonal creation by speech in Gen 1.
